title: In his image (Genesis 1:26–31)
hook: humans made in God's image, male and female, and it was very good

segments.voice: Yesterday, the days of making: spaces made, spaces filled, and your line was and it was good. What did you pause and look at after you finished it? Day three hundred thirty-four.

In the ancient world, a king couldn't be everywhere in his empire at once. So he set up statues of himself in far-off cities. Carved stone faces in the town square that told everyone who passed: this land belongs to him, his authority reaches here. An image stood in for the king. Hold that picture. Because on the sixth day, after the land animals, the story slows down. The rhythm changes. God doesn't just say let there be. God says let us make. And what gets made is a creature that carries an image. Today's word is two Latin words, and they've shaped how Christians think about every human face.
screen: `A KING'S STATUE IN A FAR-OFF TOWN.` → `THE RHYTHM CHANGES.` → `LET US MAKE.`

segments.voice: Here's verse twenty-seven in the King James Bible: "So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them." The Hebrew word for image is tselem, the same word used elsewhere in the Bible for a carved figure. The Latin is imago Dei, the image of God. Notice who's included: male and female, together, from the first line about people. Not a king, not a priest, not one special family. Every human. Scholars point to those statues of kings: in Genesis, it isn't a ruler who carries God's image into the world. It's everyone. What the image actually is, the text doesn't spell out. Christians have suggested reason, or love, or the ability to make things, or the job given in the next verse, to fill the earth and care for it as God's stand-ins. Many hold several of these at once. Another puzzle: let us make. Who is us? Many Christians, from the early church on, have heard a hint of the Trinity. Jewish readers have often heard God speaking with the heavenly court. Others hear a plural of majesty, like a royal we. The text doesn't settle it. Then the chapter ends with God looking at everything one last time: "and, behold, it was very good." Not just good, like the other days. Very good. Many Christians believe that the image has been damaged since then, but almost all of them say it has never been taken away. That's why Christians have used these verses to argue that no person can be owned, erased, or treated as nobody.
screen: `TSELEM: AN IMAGE, A CARVED FIGURE.` · `MALE AND FEMALE, EVERYONE.` · `WHAT IS THE IMAGE? WHO IS US?` · `VERY GOOD, NOT JUST GOOD.` · then, large: `IN THE IMAGE OF GOD CREATED HE HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at a face as God's image. Settle, and breathe. Bring a face to mind: someone you love, or someone you pass every day and barely see, or someone you find hard. Picture it clearly, the eyes, the lines, the expression it usually wears. Then hold the old idea up next to it: this face carries an image, like a statue in the town square. Not because of what this person has done. Just because they're human. If you pray, you can give thanks for them. The bell holds the time.
Imago Dei. Latin for the image of God, the old claim from Genesis that every human, male and female, carries God's image.
Your line: very good. Today, look one person you'd normally ignore in the face, a cashier, a driver, a neighbor, and say a real hello. Day three hundred thirty-four.

howItsDone: Many Christians ground their teaching on human dignity in the image of God, and churches across traditions cite Genesis 1:27 when speaking about the worth of every person, from the unborn to the dying, the poor and the stranger.

options: you set up a statue of yourself in the square.
fork.reveal: kings set up images of themselves. in Genesis, it isn't a ruler who carries God's image into the world. it's every human being.

original.note: Hebrew: image, used elsewhere for a carved figure. In Latin, imago Dei.

trapdoor: what you thought: made in God's image means people look like God.
what it means: every human, male and female, carries God's image into the world, and it's called very good.
what a scholar hears: tselem, a word for a carved figure, like the statues kings set up to stand in for them, given here to everyone.

notes: The royal-statue background to tselem (kings placing images in provinces) is a common scholarly reading; confirm the phrasing.
Three readings of 'let us make' (Trinity; heavenly court, common in Jewish commentary; plural of majesty) given without ranking; confirm fair description.

'Many Christians believe that the image has been damaged since then, but almost all of them say it has never been taken away': traditions differ (e.g. Reformed 'total depravity', Orthodox image/likeness distinction). Confirm wording.
'Christians have used these verses to argue that no person can be owned': imago Dei was used by abolitionists; confirm this is a fair, sourced claim (and that the script doesn't overclaim).
